f: Myokines are signaling molecules released by muscles during resistance training that cross the blood-brain barrier and directly benefit the brain. The two most important are irisin, which triggers the expression of BDNF (brain-derived neurotrophic factor) and stimulates the growth of new neurons in the hippocampus, and interleukin-6, which acts as a powerful anti-inflammatory agent during exercise and is also responsible for suppressing tumour cell growth.

What is BDNF? Brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) is a protein that supports the survival of existing neurons and encourages the growth of new ones. In the context of Alzheimer's prevention, BDNF production in the hippocampus — the brain's memory centre — is one of the most measurable neuroprotective effects of resistance training. What makes myokines so significant is not just their biological role — it's their exclusivity. Pharmaceutical companies are spending billions of dollars trying to replicate these molecules in a pill or injection and have consistently failed. The brain-protective cascade that begins when a muscle contracts under load is, so far, irreproducible outside the body. This is one of the core arguments explored in the episode, drawing on the SMART trial, which demonstrated that resistance training two to three times per week in people already experiencing mild cognitive impairment not only preserved their cognitive function but actively enhanced processing speed, fluid intelligence, and slowed grey matter loss.

The practical implication is direct: the weight room functions as a molecular pharmacy that no lab has been able to match. You can hear the full conversation, including why Bartlett describes leg strength as "by far the most important tool in your toolbox," on The Diary Of A CEO on Listenly .

— Steven Bartlett, The Diary Of A CEO

f: A 2025 Cleveland Clinic study identified a dangerous pattern called "active sedentary" — people who exercise for 30 to 60 minutes a day but then sit for 10 or more hours. The finding is stark: sitting for more than 10 hours daily increases your risk of cardiovascular disease even when you meet weekly exercise targets, because prolonged sitting shuts down lipoprotein lipase, the enzyme responsible for burning fat and clearing glucose from the blood.

What is lipoprotein lipase? Lipoprotein lipase is an enzyme that your body uses to break down fat circulating in the bloodstream and to remove glucose from the blood. When you sit for extended periods, its activity drops sharply — meaning fat and glucose accumulate in the blood even if you exercised earlier in the day. The implication is counterintuitive but well-supported: a single block of exercise in the morning does not immunize the body against the metabolic damage of sitting for the rest of the day. The two behaviors operate on separate biological mechanisms. Regular movement throughout the day keeps lipoprotein lipase active; a single workout session does not sustain that effect across the following hours of stillness.

The practical fix is surprisingly achievable. Doing 10 air squats every hour across an eight-hour workday is enough to compensate for an otherwise sedentary lifestyle — and according to the episode, this can actually outweigh the cardiovascular benefits of a single 30-minute power walk. Frequency of movement matters more than intensity when it comes to the metabolic consequences of sitting. f: In 2008, Alex Honnold free soloed Half Dome with what he admits was barely minimum preparation — and he got off route near the top, triggering extreme panic on the upper slab, which is the hardest section of the climb. Years later, while filming a documentary revisiting that same route, he attempted to walk a narrow ledge face-out above a 1,700-to-1,800-foot drop and had to bail halfway — and the two experiences were cut together in the film.

Free soloing means climbing without ropes, harnesses, or any protective equipment. Every move is unprotected: a single mistake at any point on the route is fatal. It is the highest-risk discipline in climbing, and Half Dome's upper slab — where Honnold panicked — is the technically hardest section of that particular ascent. Barely prepared, off route, and panicking 2,000 feet up

Half Dome was Alex Honnold's first major free solo. He was young, undertrained for the scale of the undertaking, and by his own admission he barely knew how to get ready for it. That level of honesty about preparation — or the lack of it — is something he discusses openly in The Diary Of A CEO with Steven Bartlett .

The critical moment came near the top of the route. Honnold got off route — meaning he lost the correct sequence of moves — and became genuinely confused on the upper slab. That section demands precise footwork and body positioning. In a roped context, confusion costs time. In a free solo context, it costs everything.

What he experienced was not just discomfort or hesitation. It was extreme panic — his word — at the exact spot where the climbing is hardest and the consequences of any error are absolute. He survived. But the experience left a mark that he later revisited on film.

f: Both Osama bin Laden and the 9/11 first responders were driven by the same dominant human need— significance —yet their choices were radically opposite. The difference lies not in the need itself, but in the beliefs they held about how to fulfill it . Bin Laden, one of approximately 27 children who felt like a nobody, sent others to die to achieve importance. The firefighters and police officers who rushed into the Twin Towers, by contrast, believed that dying as a hero made life meaningful and chose to sacrifice themselves for strangers.

This contrast reveals a fundamental principle: any human need can be met in either constructive or destructive ways, depending entirely on what someone believes is the right path. As Robbins explores in the episode , the same emotional driver—the hunger for significance—can lead one person toward evil and another toward heroism.
Belief systems determine the expression of need

Robbins emphasizes that Bin Laden and the first responders shared the psychological root: both needed to feel significant in the world . The 9/11 first responders knew entering those buildings likely meant death, yet they went anyway. Their belief system told them that dying to save others would make them heroes, making their sacrifice meaningful. For them, significance came through contribution and sacrifice.

Bin Laden, raised as one of many children in an enormous family, felt worthless. He had access to his father's vast wealth, but money alone could not give him the significance he craved. So he built a different belief: that he could become historically important by orchestrating a massive attack—not by going himself, but by commanding others to die. Both paths came from the same need, but were separated by what each person believed significance actually looked like.

This mechanism underlies much of what Robbins discusses about human behavior . The need for significance is not inherently destructive; it is the belief system attached to that need that determines whether it becomes a source of heroism or atrocity.
